summary: Deep dive on Private/VPC security architecture for a Redwood Private deployment. Discussed network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling patterns, KMS/BYOK options, audit log delivery to customer's SIEM, SOC2/ISO evidence, and pilot next steps. Agreement to exchange documentation and run a connectivity pilot to validate egress allowlisting and NAT/peering configuration.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Whitman (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (CISO, Lakemont), Tom Reynolds (Dir Infra), Maya Chen (Cloud Security Eng)
Shared links: Redwood private deployment diagram: https://redwood.app/diagrams/lakemont-vpc , SOC2 report (redacted): https://files.redwood.app/soc2/lakemont-soc2.pdf

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate you taking the time. quick roll call, and then marcus will walk through the architecture.
[00:18] Asha: hi, thanks, Asha here. im the CISO, focused on compliance, so i'll be listening for SOC2, ISO items and how logs leave your environment.
[00:26] Tom: Tom here, I'll be looking at the network side — peering, firewall, egress.
[00:31] Maya: Maya — cloud sec eng — will provide the details for ip ranges and proxies.
[00:35] Marcus: great, thanks. our goal for today is to run through the Private VPC deployment pattern, how we wire up networking, what ingress/egress looks like, and options for KMS/BYOK and logging. i'll try to call out recommended patterns and trade offs.

[00:55] Marcus: first slide, high level: Redwood Private runs a control plane that can be either customer-hosted or Redwood-managed; compute sits in your VPC in the private deployment. we support two common models: 1) VPC peering where our instances appear in your network, or 2) private endpoints/service endpoints that your VPC talks to. usually banks prefer full network isolation via peering or dedicated VPC.

[01:20] Tom: when you say peering — is that software VPC peering or transit via shared services? we have a transit gateway setup and tend to avoid cross-account peering for audit reasons.

[01:30] Marcus: yes — both are supported. for transit gateway environments we can set up attachments to the customer's TGW; alternatively, we can deploy into a customer-managed account in the case of on-prem or cloud-hosted private deployments. we also support bringing compute into your AWS account and running Redwood containers there if you'd prefer full account isolation.

[01:55] Asha: network isolation sounds good. on the compliance side we care about ingress controls and that there's no unexpected egress. specifically: can we restrict outbound egress to an allowlist and get a stable set of IPs to firewall?

[02:10] Marcus: yes — for Private we publish egress IP ranges per region for allowlisting. note — if you're using NAT in the customer's account then egress IP is your NAT; if Redwood-hosted NAT then we provide static egress IPs. we'll share the egress IP list and recommend allowlisting at the perimeter.

[02:35] Maya: do you support forcing traffic through our proxy? we use an internal HTTP proxy for monitoring.

[02:40] Marcus: we do. you can configure outbound HTTP/HTTPS to route via your proxy. we also support mutual TLS for service-to-service communication if you need mTLS.

[02:55] Lena: quick note — we have a short checklist we usually provide: egress IPs, VPC CIDR, route table needs, security group rules, and any proxy auth. we'll send that after the call.

[03:10] Tom: ok that helps. on ingress — do you require any public endpoints? we try to avoid any public-facing IPs in our zero-trust model.

[03:20] Marcus: no public ingress is required for the compute nodes. there are two options for management plane access: 1) bastion host or ssm session manager in your account for SSH/administration, or 2) a private management endpoint that we provision into your VPC. we recommend SSM or private endpoints to avoid public IPs.

[03:45] Asha: and how do you handle patching and agent updates if compute is in our account?

[03:52] Marcus: we run orchestrated updates through the control plane; if compute is in your account, we use IAM roles and assume-role flows to push updates; no inbound SSH from the internet — everything is via the management channel over private connectivity.

[04:10] Maya: can you detail firewalling at the instance level vs perimeter? we usually do defense in depth: network ACLs, security groups, and NGFW.

[04:20] Marcus: recommended pattern: perimeter NGFW enforces broad allowlists, then VPC security groups restrict by service port (e.g., 443 between internal subnets), then host-level controls (OS firewall) for extra protection. NACLs can be used for stateless filtering on the subnet boundary.

[04:45] Tom: fine-grained question — do your containers initiate outbound connections to model registries or telemetry endpoints? we want to ensure no model binaries are fetched from public internet by default.

[04:55] Marcus: by default, artifact fetching is from configured registries — in Private you can point to your internal artifact repositories or S3 endpoints. telemetry can be turned off or routed to your SIEM; by default we batch metrics outbound, but in Private we can disable telemetry or route it to customer endpoints.

[05:20] Asha: encryption: what are the KMS options? BYOK? HSM? key rotation?

[05:28] Marcus: we support multiple models: 1) Redwood-managed KMS with customer-managed keys (CMKs) in your KMS via IAM roles, 2) BYOK where you import keys into your HSM and Redwood uses them via KMS grants, and 3) local HSM in on-prem deployments. keys used for disk and object encryption can be customer-managed; we also support envelope encryption for data at rest and in transit. key rotation is supported via KMS policies; we log key usage for audit.

[05:55] Maya: do you store any plaintext customer data outside encrypted volumes?

[06:00] Marcus: no persistent plaintext. caches use encrypted storage; ephemeral memory may contain unencrypted tokens for the duration of a request but we don't persist them. we have strict memory management and wipe procedures. note: transcripts and audit logs can be routed to your S3 or SIEM to ensure you control retention.

[06:25] Asha: audit logs — we need full request/response audit trails (redacted PII) and immutable storage for 7 years for certain workflows. what does that look like?

[06:35] Marcus: we provide structured audit logs including request metadata, model, user id, response size, latency, and redaction markers. logs can be exported to customer S3 buckets or pushed to syslog/forwarder for SIEM. for immutability we support S3 object lock and write-once storage patterns if you need legal hold. retention policies can be implemented on customer side.

[07:00] Maya: how granular is RBAC? we have strict separation: engineers can deploy but not access keys, product folks can view logs but not raw customer data.

[07:10] Marcus: Redwood supports RBAC integrated with your SSO (SAML/SSO, OIDC). roles can be mapped to groups; we have fine-grained scopes for admin/ops/read-only/logs-only permissions. for Private we integrate with your IdP via SAML and can enforce SCIM for user provisioning.

[07:35] Tom: any requirements for network ACL changes on our side? we'd prefer minimal blast radius.

[07:42] Marcus: minimal: allow outbound to the egress IPs or allow peering/TGW attachment; allow inbound from the management subnet for SSM or private endpoint if using Redwood-managed control plane. otherwise pretty minimal open ports — mostly 443.

[08:00] Asha: compliance evidence — SOC2 and ISO — can you share the latest reports and scope? we need to know if Private deployment changes the scope of Redwood's SOC attestations.

[08:12] Lena: yes — i'll share our SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 certs. for Private deployments where compute runs in the customer's account, Redwood's attestation covers the control plane and processes but the customer's account responsibilities remain in scope for the bank. we'll call out the shared responsibility matrix in the doc.

[08:40] Maya: can you confirm that audit logs sent to our bucket won't be modified by Redwood? chain-of-custody is important.

[08:48] Marcus: absolutely — when we export logs to a customer-managed S3 bucket with proper IAM and object-lock, Redwood does not have write permissions. we can sign manifests of output files to verify integrity.

[09:05] Tom: network monitoring and intrusion detection — do you support forwarding PCAPs or flow logs to our SIEM?

[09:13] Marcus: we can forward VPC flow logs, application logs, and structured telemetry. PCAP is not typically forwarded due to volume, but we can provide packet-level capture on request for incident response in short windows.

[09:35] Asha: you mentioned mTLS earlier — where do you terminate TLS?

[09:40] Marcus: TLS termination usually happens at the edge in the private subnet; for mutual TLS we terminate at the load balancer in your VPC, and the backend connection between services can use mTLS too. everything is TLS1.2+ or 1.3, with cipher restrictions configurable for customers with strict crypto baselines.

[10:05] Lena: a quick callout on performance tradeoffs: some customers worry that routing through proxies or deep inspection can add latency. we recommend a pilot to measure token latency with your NGFW/proxy in the path; we can also propose an accelerated path if you want lower latency with dedicated peering.

[10:28] Tom: good point — we'll want to run a small-scale benchmark.

[10:32] Marcus: for the pilot we suggest: 1) set up TGW attachment or peering, 2) allowlist egress IPs, 3) configure audit log export to your S3, and 4) run a set of synthetic prompts to measure p99 latency. we'll provide a benchmark script.

[10:55] Maya: any specifics on firewall rules we should create? ports/protocols?

[11:00] Marcus: minimal rules: outbound 443 to egress IP list, inbound 443 from management CIDR for the management plane (if used), allow ephemeral ephemeral ports for connections initiated from the instance. we will include a proposed security group and NACL snippet in the Terraform.

[11:20] Asha: separation of environments — dev vs prod — how do you ensure data doesn't cross environments?

[11:28] Marcus: we recommend separate VPCs/subnets for dev and prod, separate KMS keys per environment, and RBAC policies that limit access. we also support account-level isolation if you need stronger separation.

[11:45] Tom: about egress — if we want to force all egress through our appliance for DLP, is there a recommended pattern?

[11:52] Marcus: yes — you can NAT via your appliance or use routing to send outbound through a proxy. if you use our Redwood-hosted NAT then we'd provide egress IPs; for full DLP you probably want appliance in your path. we can help with route table examples.

[12:15] Marcus: quick note on KV cache and model state — we persist KV cache encrypted on customer-managed storage; by default each model instance's cache is ephemeral and bound to the instance lifecycle, we don't share KV cache across customers.

[12:35] Maya: any network hardening checklists you provide?

[12:40] Lena: yes — we'll send the security checklist: network ports, IAM roles, KMS steps, SAML configuration, logging endpoints, and typical Terraform snippets.

[12:55] Asha: outstanding question: do you support customer-supplied HSM for key operations of the model weights? we have regulatory reqs around key custody.

[13:05] Marcus: short answer: yes. BYOK with customer-managed HSM is supported. for on-prem deployments we can integrate with your HSM via KMIP or HSM-specific drivers. we will need to validate performance characteristics for heavy crypto ops, but envelope encryption reduces HSM ops.

[13:30] Tom: what's the typical time to stand up a private deployment in our environment? and what resources from our infra team will you need?

[13:38] Lena: typical timeline is 4-6 weeks for a pilot (networking, IAM, KMS, basic config). resources: one infra engineer for initial peering/TGW work, a cloud security engineer for KMS and IAM review, and an SRE/ops person to run the benchmark. we'll provide step-by-step Terraform modules.

[13:58] Maya: ok that's reasonable.

[14:03] Marcus: final thing — incident response and runbooks. we provide runbooks for common IR steps and can integrate with your pagerduty. logs and traces are exportable and we can provide signed manifests for forensic integrity.

[14:20] Asha: perfect. let's recap next steps.

[14:25] Lena: recap: I'll share SOC2/ISO artifacts and the security checklist by 2026-04-02. Marcus will share the VPC diagram, Terraform snippets, and benchmark script by 2026-04-05. Maya will send us CIDRs and proxy details by 2026-04-03. we'll schedule the connectivity pilot the week of 2026-04-06.

[14:45] Tom: sounds good, thanks.
[14:48] Maya: thank you.
[14:50] Lena: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the links.

[14:55] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional recognition errors: "K V cache" for KV cache, "S S O" for SSO, minor punctuation issues.
